name: Gin Alexander
description: The original Alexander, made with gin rather than brandy — juniper against chocolate and cream, and stranger than the version that replaced it.
funFact: The gin version came first and the brandy version took the name; most bars now serve a Brandy Alexander if you order an Alexander, which reverses the history exactly.

steps: Shake all three hard with ice for 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Grate fresh nutmeg over the surface.
Serve immediately, before it separates.

name: Golden Cadillac
description: Galliano, white crème de cacao and cream — pale gold, vanilla-scented, and named for a car parked outside the bar that invented it.
funFact: Poor Red's Bar-B-Q in California claims it, named for a customer's gold Cadillac; the same bar's Golden Cadillac sales once made it one of the largest single accounts for Galliano in America.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Serve without garnish, or with a light dusting of nutmeg.
Drink while cold and still emulsified.

name: Pink Squirrel
description: Crème de noyaux, white crème de cacao and cream. Pale pink, almond-scented, and a Wisconsin supper-club fixture.
funFact: Crème de noyaux is made from apricot and peach kernels rather than almonds, and the Pink Squirrel is essentially the only drink keeping the category commercially alive.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Serve immediately.
In Wisconsin it is often blended with ice cream instead of shaken.

name: Pink Lady
description: Gin, applejack, lemon and grenadine shaken with egg white. Dismissed for decades as a ladies' drink, and considerably tougher than that suggests.
funFact: Its reputation as a soft drink is entirely a marketing artefact of the 1950s — the original is gin and applejack with a whole egg white, which is not a gentle formula.

steps: Dry-shake all ingredients without ice for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a cherry.

name: Colorado Bulldog
description: A White Russian topped with cola. The cream and the cola should fight; somehow they broker a truce.
funFact: Adding cola to a cream drink risks curdling if the cola goes in first — pour it last and gently, and the fat stays suspended.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the vodka, coffee liqueur and cream.
Stir gently to combine.
Top slowly with cola, poured down the side of the glass.
Do not stir again.

name: Godmother
description: Vodka and amaretto over a large cube. The Godfather's cleaner sibling, with the Scotch swapped out.
funFact: The 1970s duo format — one spirit, one liqueur, one big cube — produced the Godfather, Godmother, French Connection and Rusty Nail, and all four are still on menus.

steps: Put a large ice cube in a rocks glass.
Add the vodka and amaretto.
Stir gently for 10 seconds.
Serve with no garnish, or a lemon twist if it reads too sweet.

name: Toasted Almond
description: Amaretto, coffee liqueur and cream. A dessert drink that tastes exactly like its name and makes no apology for it.
funFact: Add vodka and it becomes a Roasted Toasted Almond; the 1970s cream-drink family expanded by adding a spirit and lengthening the name.

steps: Shake all ingredients with ice for 12 seconds.
Strain over fresh ice in a rocks glass.
Dust with grated nutmeg.
Serve cold.

name: Freddy Fudpucker
description: A Harvey Wallbanger built on tequila instead of vodka — orange juice with a Galliano float, and a name from the same school.
funFact: It is a straight substitution on the Wallbanger, and both drinks exist mainly because Galliano's importer spent the 1970s pushing bars to float it on things.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the tequila and top with orange juice.
Stir once to combine.
Float the Galliano over the back of a spoon.
Garnish with an orange slice.

name: Bay Breeze
description: Vodka, cranberry and pineapple. The Sea Breeze with pineapple in place of the grapefruit, and gentler for it.
funFact: The whole breeze family is vodka plus cranberry plus one other juice — grapefruit makes a Sea Breeze, pineapple a Bay Breeze, and orange a Madras.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the vodka and cranberry juice.
Top with pineapple juice.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge.

name: Madras
description: Vodka, cranberry and orange juice over ice. Named for the fabric, not the city, and the least demanding drink in any bar.
funFact: The name comes from madras plaid, whose overlapping red and orange stripes the layered juices were thought to resemble before they are stirred together.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the vodka and cranberry juice.
Float the orange juice on top without stirring.
Serve with a straw and let the drinker mix it.

name: Angel's Tip
description: Crème de cacao under a float of cream, with a cherry suspended from a pick across the rim. A pousse-café for people in a hurry.
funFact: It belongs to the pousse-café tradition of layered after-dinner drinks, a genre that largely died because it takes a steady hand and nobody has time.

steps: Pour the crème de cacao into a pony glass.
Float the cream carefully over the back of a barspoon.
Spear a cherry on a cocktail pick and rest it across the rim.
Serve immediately without stirring.

name: Velvet Hammer
description: Triple sec, crème de cacao and cream — a smoother, orange-scented cousin of the Alexander family.
funFact: Recipes differ wildly — some versions use vodka, some Tia Maria, some Cointreau — which is common for drinks that spread through hotel bars rather than books.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Serve immediately.
Dust with cocoa if you like.

name: Bitter Giuseppe
description: Cynar, sweet vermouth, lemon and orange bitters. Almost entirely bitter, served on the rocks, and a genuine test of your palate.
funFact: Stephen Cole created it at The Violet Hour in Chicago, and it is one of very few cocktails where the amaro is the base spirit rather than the modifier.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 20 seconds.
Strain over fresh ice in a rocks glass.
Garnish with a lemon twist.
Serve as a digestif rather than an aperitif.

name: Art of Choke
description: Cynar and rum with green Chartreuse, lime and mint, stirred over crushed ice. Bitter, herbal and unlike anything else.
funFact: Kyle Davidson created it at The Violet Hour; the name is a pun on artichoke, which is what Cynar is made from, and on the difficulty of getting people to order it.

steps: Press the mint gently in the bottom of a mixing glass.
Add the remaining ingredients and stir over ice for 20 seconds.
Strain over crushed ice in a rocks glass.
Garnish with a mint sprig.
Serve with a short straw.

name: Enzoni
description: A Negroni crossed with a gin sour, built on muddled grapes. Bitter, fresh and unexpectedly bright.
funFact: Created at Milk & Honey, the name splices Enzo — the grapes — with Negroni, and it converted a lot of drinkers who thought they disliked Campari.

steps: Muddle the grapes with the simple syrup in a shaker.
Add the gin, Campari, lemon juice and ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain over fresh ice in a rocks glass.
Garnish with a grape on a pick.

name: Fitzgerald
description: A gin sour with Angostura through it. Dale DeGroff's demonstration that two dashes of bitters can rebuild a whole drink.
funFact: DeGroff created it at the Rainbow Room, and it is often used to teach the point that bitters are a structural ingredient rather than a decoration.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lemon wheel.
Serve immediately.

name: Water Lily
description: Gin, crème de violette, orange liqueur and lemon — pale purple, floral and citric all at once.
funFact: Richard Boccato created it at Little Branch; crème de violette had been unavailable in America for decades and returned in 2007, immediately producing a wave of purple drinks.

steps: Shake all four in equal measure with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with an orange twist.
Serve very cold.

name: Left Hand
description: A Boulevardier with chocolate bitters — a small addition that turns the whole drink darker and rounder.
funFact: Sam Ross created it at Milk & Honey; the chocolate bitters are the only difference from a Boulevardier, and they change it more than the volume suggests they should.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a brandied cherry.
Serve cold.

name: Conference
description: Four brown spirits stirred together — bourbon, rye, cognac and calvados — with no citrus and nowhere to hide.
funFact: Named because the four spirits are 'in conference', it comes from Death & Co and is one of the stiffest modern classics in circulation.

steps: Combine all four spirits and the bitters in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for 30 seconds — this needs the dilution.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange twist over the top and discard it.

name: Bitter Mai Tai
description: A Mai Tai with Campari standing in for half the rum. Bitter, nutty and the drink that made bitter tiki a category.
funFact: Jeremy Oertel created it at Dutch Kills, and it works because orgeat's almond richness is one of very few things that can stand up to Campari without being erased.

steps: Shake all ingredients with ice for 10 seconds.
Strain over crushed ice in a rocks glass.
Garnish with a mint sprig and a spent lime shell.
Serve with a straw.

name: Cynar Julep
description: Cynar with mint and crushed ice in place of bourbon. A julep at half the strength and twice the bitterness.
funFact: Amaro juleps became a small genre in the 2010s precisely because the format — crushed ice, mint, a straw — makes a bitter liqueur approachable in a way that neat serving does not.

steps: Press the mint gently with the syrup in a julep tin.
Add the Cynar and fill the tin with crushed ice.
Swizzle until the outside of the tin frosts.
Top with more crushed ice and a splash of soda.
Garnish with a generous mint bouquet.

name: Ginger Rogers
description: Gin, mint, lime and ginger ale — a long, fresh highball named for the dancer, and much older than most people assume.
funFact: A brandy version of the name predates the gin one by decades, which is why bar books from different eras disagree entirely about what a Ginger Rogers contains.

steps: Press the mint gently in a shaker with the syrup.
Add the gin, lime juice and ice, then shake hard.
Double-strain into a highball glass filled with fresh ice.
Top with ginger ale.
Garnish with a mint sprig and a lime wheel.

name: Morgenthaler Amaretto Sour
description: The Amaretto Sour rebuilt with cask-strength bourbon and egg white — the drink that rescued a punchline.
funFact: Jeffrey Morgenthaler published it in 2012 with the argument that the Amaretto Sour was not a bad drink but a badly made one; the bourbon supplies the backbone amaretto lacks.

steps: Dry-shake all ingredients without ice for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Strain over fresh ice in a rocks glass.
Garnish with lemon peel and brandied cherries.

name: Whiskey Peach Smash
description: Bourbon muddled with fresh peach, lemon and mint over crushed ice — a summer smash that only works in season.
funFact: The smash is the most seasonal cocktail format there is — the fruit has to be ripe, which is why it appears on menus for about eight weeks a year and then vanishes.

steps: Muddle the peach wedges with the syrup and lemon juice.
Add the mint and press gently.
Add the bourbon and ice, then shake hard for 10 seconds.
Double-strain over crushed ice in a rocks glass.
Garnish with a peach slice and mint.

name: Tantris Sidecar
description: A Sidecar with green Chartreuse and apricot added — richer, herbal and considerably more complex than the original.
funFact: Created at the Tantris restaurant in Munich, it is one of very few modern classics to come out of Germany and enter the international repertoire.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lemon twist.
Serve very cold.

name: Mezcal Mule
description: A Moscow Mule with mezcal — smoke against ginger, which turns out to be one of the easier substitutions in the book.
funFact: The mule format survives almost any base spirit, which is why every distillery markets one — but ginger's heat and mezcal's smoke genuinely complement each other rather than merely coexisting.

steps: Fill a copper mug with ice.
Add the mezcal and lime juice.
Top with cold ginger beer.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge.

name: Bee Sting
description: A Bee's Knees with chilli — honey, lemon and gin with a hot edge that arrives a beat after the sweetness.
funFact: Chilli and honey work together because capsaicin is fat- and sugar-soluble — the honey carries the heat and then blunts it, which is why the burn builds and fades rather than lingering.

steps: Muddle one chilli slice gently in the shaker.
Add the gin, honey syrup, lemon juice and ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Float a thin chilli slice as garnish.
